## Where is yesterday's note?

Open the file manager and find `day01-notes.txt` by opening folders, not through
the editor's list of recent files, and write down the folders you opened, in
order. That list is the note's address. Today we learn to write such addresses
down precisely, so that you, a classmate and R can all find the seedling
measurements.

## The project as a tree

A folder can contain files and more folders, so a project can be drawn as a
tree in which indentation shows what is inside what:

```text
introcomputing-course/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── report.Rmd
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   └── seedlings.csv
├── examples/
├── output/
│   └── seedlings-practice.csv
└── reports/
    ├── day01-notes.txt
    └── file-types.txt
```

The drawing leaves out most supplied files. `data` and `reports` are neighbours:
neither is inside the other, and their **parent folder** is
`introcomputing-course`. That folder is the **project folder** (also called the
project root), the starting point for everything in the project.

In the file manager, open `reports`, go up to its parent and enter `data`, and
watch the address bar in Windows File Explorer. In Finder, choose
**View → Show Path Bar** to see the route at the bottom of the window.

## Paths

A **path** lists the folders on the route to a file, separated by `/` (or `\`
on Windows), and ends with the filename. Your username and the location of
Documents will differ from these examples:

```text
Windows: C:\Users\anna\Documents\introcomputing-course\data\seedlings.csv
Mac:     /Users/anna/Documents/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv
Linux:   /home/anna/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv
```

Read a path from left to right: start at the top of the disk (`/`, or the drive
`C:\` on Windows) and open each folder in turn.

Find out the full path of `seedlings.csv` on your own laptop. On Windows,
select the file and choose **Copy as path**; on Mac, right-click it, hold the
Option key and choose **Copy "seedlings.csv" as Pathname**. Paste the path into
a text file. It should end in `introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv`, with
your own username near the start.

## Absolute and relative paths

The paths above are **absolute**: they start at the top of the disk and give the
whole route. A **relative path** starts from a folder you have agreed on. From
the project folder, `data/seedlings.csv` means "enter `data`, then find
`seedlings.csv`". From inside `reports`, the same words ask for a `data` folder
inside `reports`, which does not exist. The folder from which a program reads
relative paths is its **working directory**; tomorrow the terminal will tell us
its working directory, and later RStudio will start in the project folder.

The absolute path contains your username and the place you chose for the
folder, so it differs on every laptop. The relative path `data/seedlings.csv` is
the same for everyone who has the project folder, which is why our R code will
use relative paths.

## Finding files from different starting folders

Use the file manager to find out which route leads from `reports` to the
practice copy `output/seedlings-practice.csv`. You have to go up to the project
folder first, because `output` is a neighbour of `reports`, not inside it.

Then make a place for notes: create a folder `practice` in the project folder,
with `field-notes` and `figures` inside it, and copy yesterday's note into
`field-notes` under the name `seedling-observations.txt`. Write down its
relative path from the project folder, close the file manager, and follow your
path to open the note again. The path is
`practice/field-notes/seedling-observations.txt`.

Names made of simple letters, numbers and hyphens, such as
`seedling-observations.txt`, say what a file holds and are easy to type in the
terminal and in R. Spaces and å, ä, ö cause trouble there.

## Saved and unsaved work

While you type, the text lives in the computer's **working memory**, which is
cleared when the program closes. **Saving** writes the text to a file on the
**disk**, where it stays after the program closes or the computer is switched
off. Use the copy `practice/field-notes/seedling-observations.txt` to see the
difference. Add "The plants were measured twice.", save, close and reopen: the
sentence is there. Then add "This line is not saved.", close the editor and
choose **Don't save**: after reopening, that line is gone. Some editors save
automatically or restore unsaved text; what counts is what is in the saved file.

## Files on other computers

A path describes a place on one computer. A cloud folder (OneDrive, iCloud) may
keep a copy elsewhere and synchronise it. Later in the course you will log into
a remote Linux computer whose folders are separate from your laptop's, even if
the names look the same, so a file is there only after you have copied it there.
For the same reason, a second copy on the same laptop is not a backup: keep
important work in the university's supported storage as well.

## What happens to a path when a folder moves?

Use the `practice` folder to find out which written routes break when a folder
is moved. Create `practice/map-a` and `practice/map-b`, and put a copy of your
note in `map-a` as `note.txt`. In a new plain-text file `reports/day02-map.txt`,
write two routes to `note.txt`: one from the project folder, and one from inside
`map-b`, which must first go up to `practice`. Write down how you expect both
routes to change, then move `map-a` into `map-b` with the file manager, follow
the routes and correct them. Open `note.txt` to see whether its contents
changed.

Finally, add to `reports/day02-map.txt` a small tree of the project folder with
`data`, `output`, `reports` and `practice`, and the relative path from the
project folder to `seedlings.csv`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: going up

From inside `map-b`, the route to `map-a` goes up one level to `practice` and
then down into `map-a`. In the terminal tomorrow, "up one level" is written `..`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your routes

Before the move, the note is at `practice/map-a/note.txt` from the project
folder, and at `../map-a/note.txt` (up to `practice`, then into `map-a`) from
inside `map-b`. After the move, it is at `practice/map-b/map-a/note.txt` from
the project folder and at `map-a/note.txt` from inside `map-b`. The contents of
`note.txt` are unchanged; only its location changed. The path to the
measurements is `data/seedlings.csv`.
:::

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## From the project folder, what is the relative path to yesterday's note?

`reports/day01-notes.txt`. From inside `reports`, its name alone is enough,
`day01-notes.txt`, because the starting point changed while the file stayed put.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why does R code in this course use `data/seedlings.csv` rather than `C:\Users\anna\…`?

The absolute path works only on Anna's laptop. The relative path works on any
computer that has the project folder, as long as R starts in that folder.
:::

**Save today:** `reports/day02-map.txt` and the `practice` folder.
